extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; aspiring philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a philosophical work (metaphysics/epistemology) presenting doctrines and methodological prescriptions (how to approach Kant, how to treat the 'world as idea').

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Kant from Kant's own works / primary-source study
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Kantian doctrine then will be sought for in vain anywhere else but in Kant’s own works; but these are throughout instructive... whoever thinks he can learn Kant’s philosophy from the exposition of others makes a terrible mistake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on second‑hand accounts or hasty lectures to learn Kant; study his original texts. The thoughts of extraordinary intellects cannot be faithfully transmitted through the 'vulgar mind'—only the authors' own works afford true insight. This is especially important before attempting more positive expositions built on Kantian foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial and distorted expositions (beware Hegelian renderings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public often seizes on expositions at second‑hand, and recent expositions (e.g., by Hegelians) can be incredible and ruinous to understanding: "How should the minds that in the freshness of youth have been strained and ruined by the nonsense of Hegelism, be still capable of following Kant’s profound investigations?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of commentators who substitute jargon, sophistry, or fashionable 'philosophemes' for genuine thought. Such accounts tend to twist, caricature, or empty original ideas; they may teach word‑combinations rather than real concepts. Prefer careful, direct study of primary texts over popular or party‑aligned summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological stance for analysis: treat presented objects as ideas (temporarily abstract from will)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of the first aspect: "In this book, however, we must consider separately that aspect of the world from which we start, its aspect as knowable, and therefore, in the meantime, we must, without reserve, regard all presented objects, even our own bodies ... merely as ideas, and call them merely ideas. By so doing we always abstract from will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing the world 'as idea', adopt the explicit methodological move of treating perceivable objects (including the body) as ideas—i.e., as objects of consciousness—while temporarily abstracting from 'will'. This focused abstraction is provisional and will be corrected or complemented in subsequent discussion (the 'world as will').

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for authentic philosophy: pursuit of truth vs. professional motives
rubrics_metrics.description: True philosophy seeks 'truth alone' and may not permit a livelihood, whereas professorial or 'university' philosophy is shaped by external aims: "the fear of the Lord, the will of the ministry, the laws of the established church, the wishes of the publisher, the attendance of the students, the goodwill of colleagues, the course of current politics..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating philosophical work or orientations, distinguish those motivated primarily by honest search for truth (possibly uncompromising and not 'livable') from those shaped by institutional, political, ecclesiastical, or commercial incentives. Expect different styles, compromises, and emphases from each; recognize that 'professorial' philosophy may ignore or 'secret' what threatens its usefulness or patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer author's original chapters for insight over secondary expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principal chapters of any one of these true philosophers will afford a thousand times more insight into their doctrines than the heavy and distorted accounts of them that everyday men produce..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For genuine understanding, read the principal chapters of primary authors rather than relying on popular or stylized summaries. Primary chapters convey the author's own conceptual structure and are more instructive even where the author 'errs' or 'fails.'
